questions.subtopic: Case Study 1: Rice Cultivation in Canal-Irrigated Regions
questions.question: According to the NCERT chapter's textbook statement, India is which largest producer of rice after China?
options: Second largest producer
First largest producer
Tenth largest producer
Fifth largest producer
questions.explanation: This question asks for the older NCERT textbook statement, which describes India as the world's second-largest rice producer after China. It must not be presented as a current ranking: Government of India publications are inconsistent: one PIB release describes India as the world's largest rice producer, while another PIB release/backgrounder describes India as second-largest despite citing 150.18 million tonnes. The ranking therefore remains a source discrepancy; the answer is retained only as a dated textbook-text recall and must not be presented as a settled current ranking.

questions.question: Case Study 2 (Continued): How do millets demonstrate high climate resilience compared to rice and wheat?

They are drought-hardy, rain-fed crops that thrive on poor shallow soils with minimal irrigation and can withstand high temperatures
They can survive without any carbon dioxide
They absorb water directly from lightning strikes

questions.question: Case Study 3 (Q17-Q18): Tea cultivation is an example of plantation agriculture in India.\n\nQ17: Why are tea processing factories invariably located right within or adjacent to the tea gardens?
options: Because tea leaves explode if exposed to road vibrations
Tender tea leaves lose their fresh aroma, moisture, and quality quickly if transported over long distances before wilting and drying
To prevent wild elephants from drinking the tea
Because British laws prohibited moving tea outside garden gates
questions.explanation: Tea processing (withering, rolling, fermenting, drying) must begin immediately after plucking to lock in the volatile aromatic oils and prevent spoilage.
